<p class="hs-banner" role="note"><strong>Simulated data · experimental genomic route · count stays 7.</strong>
This page fits data whose truth is known, so you can see what the genomic route recovers. It is development evidence on one simulation design. It does not flip a <code>validation_status</code> row, and the GWAS p-values are nominal, not genome-wide calibrated.</p>

This case study simulates a genotyped, pedigreed population with a polygenic
trait of known heritability. It then asks three questions of `hsquared`:

1. Does genomic GREML, `genomic(1 | id, markers = M)`, recover the simulated
   heritability, and are its standard errors the right size?
2. Do genomic breeding values (GEBVs) predict the true genetic values better
   than pedigree EBVs?
3. Does a relatedness-corrected marker scan, `gwas()`, find the causal SNPs?

The code is shown but not run when this site is built. Fitting needs a local
Julia, `JuliaCall` and `HSquared.jl`. The numbers and figures come from running
the same code once; the scripts are in `dev-test/genomic-sim/` in the source
repository.

## The simulated population

The simulator is a gene drop through a pedigree, written in base R:

- 200 unrelated founders, with allele frequencies drawn from U(0.05, 0.95);
- 5 discrete generations of 400 offspring each, from random sires and dams of
  the previous generation, so half-sibs, full-sibs and cousins arise;
- 10 chromosomes of 1 Morgan with 1,000 SNPs each, and Haldane meiosis, so
  linked markers are in linkage disequilibrium within families;
- 200 causal SNPs with normal effects, scaled so that the genetic variance
  among the 2,000 phenotyped animals is 0.4;
- `y = 10 + 0.5 * male + g + e`, with `Var(e) = 0.6`, so the simulated
  heritability is **h² = 0.4**.

The 200 founders are genotyped but not phenotyped. Markers that are
monomorphic in the phenotyped animals are dropped.

<details>
<summary>The simulator, <code>simulate_population()</code> (about 100 lines of base R)</summary>

```{r simulator}
simulate_population <- function(seed = 1, n_founders = 200, n_gen = 5,
                                n_per_gen = 400, n_chr = 10,
                                snps_per_chr = 1000, n_causal = 200,
                                h2 = 0.4, sex_effect = 0.5) {
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- n_chr * snps_per_chr
  chr <- rep(seq_len(n_chr), each = snps_per_chr)
  pos <- unlist(lapply(seq_len(n_chr), function(i) sort(runif(snps_per_chr))))
  chr_idx <- split(seq_len(m), chr)

  n_total <- n_founders + n_gen * n_per_gen
  hap1 <- matrix(as.raw(0), n_total, m)
  hap2 <- matrix(as.raw(0), n_total, m)
  p0 <- runif(m, 0.05, 0.95)
  hap1[seq_len(n_founders), ] <- as.raw(matrix(
    runif(n_founders * m) < rep(p0, each = n_founders), n_founders))
  hap2[seq_len(n_founders), ] <- as.raw(matrix(
    runif(n_founders * m) < rep(p0, each = n_founders), n_founders))

  id <- character(n_total); sire <- dam <- rep(NA_character_, n_total)
  sex <- character(n_total); gen <- integer(n_total)
  id[seq_len(n_founders)] <- sprintf("F%04d", seq_len(n_founders))
  sex[seq_len(n_founders)] <- rep(c("M", "F"), length.out = n_founders)

  # one gamete: Poisson(1) crossovers per chromosome (Haldane)
  gamete <- function(parent) {
    out <- raw(m)
    for (k in seq_len(n_chr)) {
      idx <- chr_idx[[k]]
      ncross <- rpois(1, 1)
      start_hap <- sample(2L, 1)
      if (ncross == 0) {
        out[idx] <- if (start_hap == 1) hap1[parent, idx] else hap2[parent, idx]
      } else {
        seg <- findInterval(pos[idx], sort(runif(ncross)))
        from1 <- (seg %% 2 == 0) == (start_hap == 1)
        h <- hap2[parent, idx]
        h[from1] <- hap1[parent, idx][from1]
        out[idx] <- h
      }
    }
    out
  }

  prev <- seq_len(n_founders)
  nxt <- n_founders
  for (g in seq_len(n_gen)) {
    sires <- prev[sex[prev] == "M"]; dams <- prev[sex[prev] == "F"]
    kids <- nxt + seq_len(n_per_gen)
    for (j in kids) {
      s <- sires[sample.int(length(sires), 1)]
      d <- dams[sample.int(length(dams), 1)]
      hap1[j, ] <- gamete(s)
      hap2[j, ] <- gamete(d)
      sire[j] <- id[s]; dam[j] <- id[d]
    }
    id[kids] <- sprintf("G%d_%04d", g, seq_len(n_per_gen))
    sex[kids] <- sample(c("M", "F"), n_per_gen, replace = TRUE)
    gen[kids] <- g
    prev <- kids; nxt <- max(kids)
  }

  M <- matrix(as.integer(hap1) + as.integer(hap2), n_total, m)
  rownames(M) <- id
  colnames(M) <- sprintf("chr%d_%04d", chr, ave(chr, chr, FUN = seq_along))
  rm(hap1, hap2)

  rec <- which(gen > 0)
  seg <- which(apply(M[rec, , drop = FALSE], 2, function(x) any(x != x[1])))
  M <- M[, seg, drop = FALSE]; chr <- chr[seg]; pos <- pos[seg]

  causal <- sort(sample(ncol(M), n_causal))
  beta <- rnorm(n_causal)
  g_all <- drop(scale(M[, causal, drop = FALSE], scale = FALSE) %*% beta)
  k <- sqrt(h2 / var(g_all[rec]))
  beta <- beta * k; g_all <- g_all * k
  y <- 10 + sex_effect * (sex == "M") + g_all + rnorm(n_total, sd = sqrt(1 - h2))

  pheno <- data.frame(id = id, sex = factor(sex), generation = gen, y = y,
                      true_g = g_all)[rec, ]
  rownames(pheno) <- NULL
  list(
    pheno = pheno,
    pedigree = data.frame(id = id, dam = dam, sire = sire),
    markers = M, # all 2,200 animals, 0/1/2 allele counts
    map = data.frame(marker = colnames(M), chr = chr, pos = pos,
                     causal = seq_len(ncol(M)) %in% causal,
                     effect = replace(numeric(ncol(M)), causal, beta)),
    truth = list(h2 = h2, var_g = var(g_all[rec]), var_e = 1 - h2)
  )
}
```

</details>

```{r simulate}
library(hsquared)
sim <- simulate_population(seed = 1) # a few seconds
dat <- sim$pheno                     # 2,000 phenotyped animals
M <- sim$markers[dat$id, ]           # their genotypes: 2,000 x 10,000
dim(sim$markers)
#> [1]  2200 10000
```

The marker matrix holds allele counts `0`/`1`/`2`, one row per animal, with the
animal IDs as row names. That is the coding `genomic(markers = M)` expects (see
[Genomic prediction](genomic-prediction.html)).

## Genomic heritability

Fit genomic GREML from the markers. The engine builds the VanRaden genomic
relationship matrix and estimates the genomic and residual variances by
AI-REML:

```{r fit-genomic}
fit_g <- hsquared(
  y ~ sex + genomic(1 | id, markers = M),
  data = dat,
  family = gaussian(),
  REML = TRUE,
  control = hs_control(
    engine = "julia",
    engine_control = list(target = "genomic")
  )
)
variance_components(fit_g)
heritability(fit_g)
heritability_standard_error(fit_g)
```

For comparison, fit the ordinary pedigree animal model to the same animals:

```{r fit-pedigree}
fit_a <- hsquared(
  y ~ sex + animal(1 | id, pedigree = sim$pedigree),
  data = dat,
  family = gaussian(),
  REML = TRUE
)
heritability(fit_a)
heritability_standard_error(fit_a)
```

On this replicate (seed 1):

| | Genomic GREML | Pedigree animal model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Genetic variance | 0.353 | 0.322 |
| Residual variance | 0.611 | 0.645 |
| h² | 0.366 | 0.333 |
| SE of h² | 0.035 | 0.038 |
| 95% delta-method interval | 0.301 to 0.436 | 0.264 to 0.410 |

The realised heritability in this sample, the variance of the true genetic
values over the variance of `y` after removing the sex effect, is 0.414.

`heritability(fit_g)` labels its estimate `genomic_variance_ratio` on the
`K_lambda` scale: the engine adds a small ridge (0.01) to the genomic
relationship matrix, and the ratio is defined relative to that matrix.

Both estimates fall below the simulated 0.4 on this replicate. One replicate
cannot tell you whether an estimator is biased, so the next section repeats
the whole simulation.

The standard errors are inverse average-information SEs, the convention used by
ASReml, WOMBAT and BLUPF90 and the `hsquared` default
(`hs_control(se_method = "ai")`). Pass `se_method = "observed"` for SEs from the
observed information instead.

## Does it recover h² across replicates?

The simulation and both fits were repeated for seeds 1 to 20. All 20 genomic fits
converged.

```{r genomic-sim-h2-recovery, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = "asis"}
cat(sprintf(
  '<p><img src="../reference/figures/genomic-sim-h2-recovery.svg" class="r-plt" alt="%s" width="100%%"></p>\n',
  "Heritability estimates for 20 simulated replicates, each shown as a genomic GREML estimate and a pedigree animal-model estimate with 1.96-standard-error bars, against the simulated value of 0.4. Both sets scatter around 0.4; the genomic bars are slightly shorter."
))
```

| | Genomic GREML | Pedigree animal model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mean h² (simulated 0.4) | 0.408 | 0.403 |
| Bias ± Monte Carlo SE | +0.008 ± 0.008 | +0.003 ± 0.010 |
| SD of the 20 estimates | 0.035 | 0.043 |
| Mean reported SE | 0.034 | 0.038 |
| Estimate ± 1.96 SE covers 0.4 | 19 / 20 | 19 / 20 |

Three things to read from this:

- **No detectable bias.** Both means are within one Monte Carlo SE of 0.4.
- **The genomic SEs are the right size.** The average reported SE (0.034)
  matches the spread of the estimates across replicates (0.035). For the
  pedigree model the reported SE is about 10% smaller than the spread; with 20
  replicates that difference is within noise.
- **Genomic estimates are more precise.** Their spread is about 20% smaller than
  the pedigree estimates', because the markers measure realised relationships,
  including the Mendelian-sampling deviations a pedigree can only average over.

Twenty replicates are enough to see gross bias or badly sized SEs. They are not
enough to calibrate interval coverage: 19 / 20 has a binomial SE of about 5
percentage points.

## Breeding values

Both fits return breeding values for every phenotyped animal. Because the
simulation knows each animal's true genetic value, you can score them directly:

```{r breeding-values}
gebv <- breeding_values(fit_g)
ebv <- breeding_values(fit_a)
cor(gebv$value[match(dat$id, gebv$id)], dat$true_g)
cor(ebv$value[match(dat$id, ebv$id)], dat$true_g)
```

```{r genomic-sim-gebv, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = "asis"}
cat(sprintf(
  '<p><img src="../reference/figures/genomic-sim-gebv.png" class="r-plt" alt="%s" width="100%%"></p>\n',
  "Two scatter plots of predicted breeding value against true genetic value for 2,000 animals in replicate 1: genomic GBLUP on the left and pedigree BLUP on the right, each with a one-to-one line and its correlation in the panel title."
))
```

Across the 20 replicates the GEBV accuracy averaged 0.765 and the EBV accuracy
0.743. GEBVs were more accurate in every replicate, by 0.016 to 0.031. The gain
is small here because every phenotyped animal also has its own record and a
deep pedigree; genomic prediction gains most for animals without records.

## Finding the causal SNPs

`gwas()` scans the markers one at a time with a mixed-model (GLS) Wald test.
It uses the variance components and pedigree relationship matrix of a fitted
animal model to correct for relatedness, so it takes the pedigree fit `fit_a`.
The marker matrix must cover every animal in the pedigree, founders included,
in any row order with IDs as row names:

```{r gwas}
scan <- gwas(fit_a, sim$markers)
head(scan[order(scan$p_value), ])
```

```{r genomic-sim-manhattan, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE, results = "asis"}
cat(sprintf(
  '<p><img src="../reference/figures/genomic-sim-manhattan.png" class="r-plt" alt="%s" width="100%%"></p>\n',
  "Manhattan plot of minus log10 p-values for 10,000 SNPs on 10 chromosomes in replicate 1. The 200 causal SNPs are highlighted; the handful of SNPs above the Bonferroni line are causal SNPs."
))
```

On seed 1, six SNPs pass the Bonferroni line, and all six are causal. The
twelve smallest p-values all belong to causal SNPs, and so do all nine SNPs
with a Benjamini-Hochberg q-value below 0.05.

Over the 20 replicates, an average of 5.8 SNPs per replicate passed the
Bonferroni line, and 114 of those 116 were causal. Power is low because 200 causal SNPs share a heritability of 0.4, so most
effects are small; this is a polygenic trait, not a major-gene one.

The genomic-control inflation factor λ averaged 1.10 (range 1.05 to 1.14). For
a polygenic trait with long-range linkage in families some inflation reflects
real signal, so λ alone is not evidence of miscalibration here. As the
[GWAS status page](qtl-gwas-eqtl-status.html) says, the scan's p-values and
Bonferroni line are nominal, not a validated genome-wide threshold.

## Running time

| Step (seed 1) | Seconds |
| --- | --- |
| Simulate the population | 2 |
| Pedigree animal model, 2,000 animals | 0.5 |
| Genomic GREML, 2,000 animals × 10,000 SNPs | 14 |
| `gwas()` scan of 10,000 SNPs | 14 |

Times are from one R session on an Apple-silicon laptop, after Julia had
started. The first `hsquared()` call in a session also starts Julia and
compiles the engine, which adds about 18 seconds.

If you run replicates in parallel, give each process one BLAS thread. Julia's
BLAS uses every core by default, and several processes each doing that slowed
these fits down 5 to 50 times. Set it once per R session, after the first fit
has started Julia:

```{r blas-threads}
JuliaCall::julia_command("using LinearAlgebra; BLAS.set_num_threads(1)")
```

Or set the environment variable `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` before R starts.

## What this does and does not show

It shows that, on this design, genomic GREML recovers the simulated
heritability without detectable bias, that its standard errors match the
replicate-to-replicate spread, and that the marker scan finds causal SNPs with
very few false hits.

It does not show:

- **Coverage.** Twenty replicates cannot calibrate interval coverage.
- **Other designs.** One population structure, one marker density and one
  genetic architecture were tested. There were no rare variants, no founder LD,
  no selection and no imputation errors.
- **Genome-wide significance.** The scan p-values are nominal.
- **A validation-status change.** The genomic route stays experimental, and
  `public_covered_count` stays 7.

For the other genomic paths (supplied `Ginv`, SNP-BLUP, single-step), see
[Genomic prediction](genomic-prediction.html).
